Qatar’s New Tariff on Logistics Equipment Sends Ripples Through Industry Operations

Qatar’s recently imposed 18% tariff on imported logistics equipment, including cargo handling machinery and warehouse automation systems, is having immediate and far-reaching effects on the country’s Transportation & Logistics industry. The measure, announced by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry on June 4, was justified by officials as a step to “bolster local industrial capabilities and reduce import dependence.” However, industry stakeholders report mounting operational challenges and uncertainty as the new tariff takes effect.

The impact is being felt across the sector, from large logistics firms managing distribution hubs near Doha to smaller freight handlers operating along the Ras Laffan corridor. Khalid Al-Mansoori, CEO of Gulf Transit Solutions, said, “We rely on timely upgrades to our cargo handling systems to maintain efficiency. The added cost from this tariff is forcing us to reconsider planned investments and scale back modernization efforts.”

Many industry players had ongoing procurement contracts for new cranes, conveyor belts, and warehouse robotics scheduled for delivery this quarter. With the tariff applied at the point of entry, several firms are now facing significant price increases—some reporting cost hikes of up to 22% after factoring in additional fees and currency shifts. “We’re already delaying installation of new equipment at our Mesaieed facility,” said Fatima Al-Suwaidi, operations director at Q-Logix, a regional freight company. “This means our teams are working overtime to keep up with demand using older systems.”

The industry’s trade association, Qatar Logistics Forum, issued a statement urging authorities to reconsider the tariff, warning that “reduced investment in logistics infrastructure could undermine the sector’s competitiveness and limit job creation for Qatari nationals and residents.” According to the Forum, the sector employs approximately 38,000 workers, with an estimated 4,500 positions directly involved in equipment maintenance and operation.

In the short term, logistics firms report a slowdown in expansion projects and upgrades at key sites. Some companies are reviewing their capital expenditure plans for the year, while others are seeking temporary solutions such as leasing equipment from local suppliers rather than purchasing new units from abroad. Several managers expressed concern about potential productivity declines if aging machinery remains in service longer than anticipated.

The Ministry of Commerce and Industry has indicated it will monitor the effects of the tariff over the next six months, but has not signaled any intention to adjust the policy. “Our priority is fostering a robust local supply chain,” a ministry spokesperson said. “We are in dialogue with industry stakeholders and will continue to assess the situation.”

As the tariff continues to reshape the operational landscape for Qatar’s Transportation & Logistics industry, firms and workers alike are bracing for a period of adjustment and uncertainty.
